The grid’s next hidden gate is proving that the model matches the plant

The familiar obstacles to building a power plant are physical and procedural: transmission upgrades, transformer lead times, land, permits, deposits, financing and the interconnection queue.

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-06-21 · Updated 2026-06-28 · 12 min read

In brief

  • 1,178 MW | Blue Cut showed a cleared fault could still erase solar output.
  • 2,060 GW | generation and storage remained in U.S. interconnection queues at end-2025.
  • April 2026 | two new NERC model-verification standards became effective.
  • 2028–2029 | later data and operational standards extend the implementation sequence.
  • One delayed project | would turn model credibility from compliance work into a proven bottleneck.

A project reaches this gate after clearing the visible ones

Utility-scale photovoltaic plant

A solar plant is no longer just steel, glass, and land; it is also a control system the grid must be able to model.

A solar or battery project can work through those problems and still encounter another gate. Before a transmission planner relies on the facility, the project may need to show that its submitted model reproduces how the installed inverters and plant controller will behave during faults, weak-grid conditions and voltage or frequency excursions.

That creates a sequential workflow:

late-stage IBR project → applicable model requirement → RMS or EMT representation → verification against test or disturbance data → planner acceptance

The operative word is applicable. Current requirements do not force every inverter-based resource to submit a bespoke electromagnetic-transient model. Facility class, voltage, size, regional practice, planner judgment, study need, generic-model allowances and legacy exclusions determine the burden.

The strongest version of the thesis is therefore narrower than “models are the grid’s next national bottleneck.” It is that model credibility is becoming a differentiated acceptance gate for some projects, especially in high-IBR systems and in cases where conventional positive-sequence studies cannot represent the relevant control behavior.

The evidence supports the technical mechanism. It does not yet establish widespread project delays, repeat procurement or a distinct high-margin market. The system is in early deployment, before repeatable commercial practice.

Disturbance reports changed what planners need to prove

The reason this issue persists is that several major grid events exposed a gap between expected and actual inverter behavior.

During the 2016 Blue Cut disturbance in Southern California, faults on the transmission system were followed by approximately 1,178 MW of solar photovoltaic reduction. The affected facilities were not simply disconnected by the faulted equipment. Their controls responded to the disturbance in ways that produced a large aggregate loss. (NERC Blue Cut report)

The 2017 Canyon 2 events involved approximately 682 MW and 937 MW of photovoltaic interruption. Investigators found that one erroneous frequency-tripping mechanism identified after Blue Cut appeared to have been corrected, but momentary cessation and delayed restoration remained important. The lesson was not that every event had the same cause. It was that settings, restoration dynamics and model assumptions had to be checked rather than inferred. (NERC Canyon 2 report)

The 2021 Odessa disturbance in ERCOT produced approximately 1,340 MW of reductions. Some affected facilities were about 200 miles from the initiating fault. NERC concluded that some of the observed issues should have been examined before interconnection, making Odessa the clearest link between field behavior and the quality of pre-operational studies. (NERC Odessa report)

A joint NERC, WECC and CAISO report later examined four qualifying Western Interconnection events from March through June 2024. The recurrence matters more than mechanical uniformity. Years of guidance and remediation had not eliminated widespread inverter-output reductions during bulk-power disturbances. (2024 Western disturbance report)

The rules are tightening in stages, not all at once

FERC Order No. 901 directed NERC to address four related gaps: data sharing, model validation, planning and operational studies, and inverter performance. That moved the issue from technical guidance toward formal reliability regulation. (FERC Order No. 901)

FERC approved a new modeling and data package in February 2026, but the standards do not take effect on one common date.

MOD-026-2 and MOD-033-3 became effective on April 1, 2026. MOD-026-2 addresses dynamic-model requirements and verification documentation for applicable facilities. MOD-033-3 covers validation of planning models against actual system behavior.

MOD-032-2 follows on April 1, 2028. IRO-010-6 and TOP-003-8 follow on April 1, 2029, extending the sequence into model-data collection and operational information.

That calendar matters. A February 2026 approval headline can sound like an immediate national mandate. The actual implementation path is phased, scope-dependent and mediated by regional procedures.

The framework also contains relief valves. Legacy facilities may retain EMT-model exclusions where vendor support is unavailable or the planner does not identify the facility. Generic models may be accepted in some comparable cases. Those provisions limit the near-term workload while demonstrating that regulators are already balancing model fidelity against practical feasibility.

IEEE adds a second layer. IEEE 2800-2022 supplies common technical requirements for large inverter-based resources. IEEE 2800.2-2026 adds recommended procedures for plant-level conformity assessment. The newer document advances the system from defining required behavior toward testing whether a plant conforms, but it is not itself a universal mandatory project gate.

The commercial product is an evidence chain, not a software file

A credible model package depends on several actors whose records may not align.

The inverter or wind-turbine OEM controls proprietary control logic. A plant power controller introduces site-specific settings. The developer or consultant assembles RMS and EMT representations. The planner provides the network cases and acceptance criteria. Field instruments and plant historians supply measured behavior. A laboratory may test physical or emulated controllers in real time.

The relevant commercial chain is therefore broader than a PSCAD or PSS/E file:

equipment version → firmware → plant settings → RMS model → EMT model → test case → measured response → discrepancy analysis → planner approval

Every handoff can create rework.

An OEM model may reflect a different firmware release from the equipment installed at the site. A plant controller may be retuned after the interconnection study. A consultant and planner may use different software versions or network cases. Field measurements may lack the resolution needed to validate fast control behavior.

DNV currently offers model development and validation across ASPEN OneLiner, PowerFactory, PSLF, PSCAD/EMTDC, MATLAB Simulink and Siemens PSS/E. Siemens, PSCAD and RTDS provide parts of the simulation and testing infrastructure. RTDS also documents PSCAD-to-real-time and hardware-in-the-loop workflows. These offerings prove that a supplier ecosystem exists. They do not prove a large or scarce market. (DNV model development) (RTDS co-simulation)

DOE’s i2X roadmap identifies training and engineering-capacity concerns around advanced interconnection studies. It does not provide an industry-wide workforce dataset, so the evidence supports a specialized skill requirement rather than a measured national labour shortage.

Control may matter more than the size of the service market

Several parties could capture value if model verification becomes a recurring gate.

OEMs hold the most important proprietary information. They can bundle black-box models, grid-code support, firmware updates and lifecycle services into equipment contracts. That may deepen customer dependence without creating a separate public revenue line.

Simulation vendors control installed software environments, file formats, model libraries and user workflows. Licences and maintenance can recur even when consulting work is commoditized.

Engineering firms can earn project fees by translating between OEM data, plant settings and planner requirements. Their leverage depends on whether the work remains bespoke. Standardized IEEE procedures and common-model libraries could expand the number of required submissions while reducing the engineering effort per project.

Hardware-in-the-loop providers and laboratories benefit only when static models are insufficient. Their economics depend on accepted test protocols, laboratory utilization and test-slot scarcity—none of which is established in the current public record.

Utilities and RTOs may absorb much of the spending internally. They own the acceptance workflow, understand the network cases and can build permanent review teams. Internal hiring is cost migration, not external market expansion.

The most durable control point may remain institutional. FERC and NERC establish obligations, but regional planners decide applicability, acceptable evidence and whether a discrepancy blocks a project milestone.

That is why technical importance should not be confused with independent pricing power. The workflow can grow while OEMs, utilities and established engineering firms retain the customer relationship and margin.

The strongest counterargument is that this becomes routine compliance

The central thesis can fail even while every technical claim remains true.

Transmission upgrades, equipment lead times, permitting, deposits and financing may continue to determine project schedules. Model discrepancies may be resolved inside ordinary study cycles without affecting commercial-operation dates. Regulators may implement the new standards through existing data systems and audit procedures.

Standardization could also outrun scarcity.

IEEE 2800.2 may turn plant-level conformity assessment into a repeatable test process. EPRI and other common-model initiatives may give planners acceptable representations for defined project classes. OEMs may improve ride-through settings and grid-forming controls faster than disturbance-driven validation demand grows.

Canyon 2 provides a partial historical base rate. A specific erroneous frequency-tripping mechanism identified after Blue Cut appeared to have been corrected through settings and OEM remediation. The same episode also showed that new concerns—momentary cessation and restoration—could remain after one defect was fixed.

What is similar now is the cycle of disturbance, investigation, guidance, remediation and formalization. What is different is the scale of inverter-based development and the movement of model verification into enforceable standards.

A clean counterexample would be especially valuable: a late-stage project that completed demanding facility-specific validation quickly, at routine cost and without schedule impact. Public event reports tend to document failures more readily than successful qualification, so the available evidence may overrepresent exceptional cases.

What would turn the workflow into a commercial gate

The standards themselves are not the decisive evidence.

The first meaningful threshold is a named project whose interconnection, commissioning or continued-operation milestone cannot close until a model discrepancy is corrected and accepted.

The second is recurrence. Two unrelated facilities completing documented discrepancy-correction-acceptance cycles would show that the process is not an isolated engineering fix.

The third is contractual risk transfer. An OEM, EPC or project agreement would need to assign responsibility for model delivery, firmware-to-model updates, validation support and remedies for non-performance.

The fourth is recognized commercial demand: recurring procurement, provider backlog or revenue specifically attributed to IBR modeling and validation rather than embedded inside broader equipment or engineering scopes.

Those thresholds separate a real reliability workflow from a distinct commercialization bottleneck.

What to watch

  • 2027-12-31: a major grid operator mandates a defined EMT or equivalent artifact for a specified IBR class.
  • 2027-12-31: NERC or a regional entity publishes IBR-specific model-verification audit evidence guidance.
  • 2028-12-31: a named project discloses a milestone delay caused by model fidelity or failed validation.
  • 2029-12-31: two independent facilities complete documented model correction-and-acceptance cycles.
  • 2030-12-31: an OEM or EPC contract discloses enforceable model-delivery and update obligations.
  • 2030-12-31: a provider reports recurring IBR-validation procurement, backlog or attributable revenue.

The conclusion is a regional gate, not a national shortage

The grid already has a model-verification problem. Disturbance reports show that installed inverter behavior can diverge from planning assumptions, and regulators are converting parts of model integrity into auditable obligations.

The unresolved question is commercial bindingness.

For now, model credibility is best understood as a sequential gate that some late-stage projects encounter after navigating more visible physical and procedural constraints. It is most likely to matter first in high-IBR regions and difficult control environments during the 2026–2029 implementation window.

The thesis strengthens when a named project milestone is withheld pending model correction and later closes after validation. It weakens if regional operators absorb the standards through existing processes, generic models cover most projects and delays continue to come overwhelmingly from transmission, equipment, permitting and finance.

Until that settlement event appears, validated models are an increasingly important part of grid reliability—but not yet a proven national bottleneck or a distinct high-margin market.
